..Today through Tuesday...Tropical Storm Rachel, about
500 miles southwest of San Diego as of 8 AM MST, is quickly moving
northward as it begins to be pulled northward by an upper-level 
low off the California coast. As this occurs, tropical moisture is
expected to increase across much of Arizona through the day. PHX 
ACARS profiles have already begun to show around a 0.2 inch increase
in PWATs this morning vs yesterday afternoon. 

As a result, scattered showers and thunderstorms look to overspread 
the region from southwest to northeast starting late this morning 
into the afternoon hours. The most favored area for storms looks to 
mainly be across western Arizona, as an upper-level jet looks to 
develop by this afternoon to provide large-scale ascent to support 
precipitation development. 

The remnants of Rachel are expected to make landfall late tonight or 
early Sunday morning around northern Baja, before moving along the 
Arizona-California border. Moisture looks to peak across Arizona 
around this time, with model soundings showing a nearly saturated 
profile. The upper-level jet looks to become an enhanced over 
Arizona at the same time, as deepening trough digs into the western 
US. As a result, more widespread coverage of showers and 
thunderstorms are expected late tonight into much of Sunday. Gusty 
southerly winds are also expected, likely enhancing precipitation 
amounts in the upslope areas. While at the same time, enhanced 
downsloping will likely lead to rain shadowing of areas north and 
east of the Mogollon Rim.

By Monday and Tuesday, drier air begins to move in aloft as the main 
low moves into Arizona. However, model soundings still show plenty 
of residual shallow moisture, which combined with strong orographic 
lift will keep scattered showers and thunderstorms in place across 
the higher terrain. 

Overall, the greatest threat from this system will be flash 
flooding, especially in rain sensitive locations such as burn scars 
and slot canyons. Their remains some uncertainty with how widespread 
the risk will be, as much of the area may see a more steady, light 
to moderate rainfall. However, where the areas of embedded heavy 
rainfall setup will see a higher flash flood risk. Latest HREF and 
REFS guidance show the greatest potential for heavy rainfall to be 
across Yavapai and Gila counties early Sunday morning and peaking by 
the afternoon hours. A Flash Flood Watch is in effect for much of 
the Mogollon Rim and south to cover this threat, along with the 
Grand Canyon and Page areas to cover the burn scar and slot canyon 
risk.

The threat for severe thunderstorms does increase given the added 
wind shear, however the amount of instability over the region 
remains in question and will be the limiting factor. Damaging winds 
would be the main threat with any severe storm, however, an isolated 
tornado can not be totally ruled out in any stronger, more organized 
storm. The greatest risk looks to be across central Arizona on Sunday,
however confidence in this threat is low given the potential lack
of daytime heating.

Wednesday through Friday...Model solution begin to diverge by the 
middle of the week. The GFS lifts the trough north and east out of 
Arizona and into the northern US, with a weak cut-off low developing 
off northern Baja. The ECMWF on the other hand favors the low 
breaking off from the jet, and remaining stationary over the Four 
Corners region. The EPS and GEFS means both seem to favor their 
operational counterpart, though the run-to-run trend in the GEFS 
does signal towards a slower departure of the low.

The current NBM forecast through the extended period favors a 
gradually warming trend, with gusty northeasterly winds developing, 
which seems reasonable. There remain some precip chances, mainly 
across eastern Arizona, but these might be slightly on the lower end 
(especially on Wednesday). However, given the high amount of model 
disagreement, confidence in the later-half of the week remains very 
low at this point in time.
